state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Actually, alternate angles are not always equal. Alternate angles are equal only when the lines intersected by a transversal are parallel. In this case, the lines are not parallel, so angles \( p \) and \( q \) are not necessarily equal. Can you think of a way to prove whether Tom or Katie is correct in this scenario?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it a bit better now. So, if the lines aren't parallel, then the alternate angles can be different, right? But how do I know if two lines are parallel just by looking at them?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track! To determine if two lines are parallel just by looking at them, you can look for specific angle relationships. One way is to check if corresponding angles are equal. If corresponding angles are equal, then the lines are parallel. Can you think of any other angle relationships that can help us determine if the lines are parallel?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, okay! So if I check for corresponding angles and they're equal, then the lines are parallel. But what if I can't see any corresponding angles? Are there other ways to tell if the lines are parallel, or do I just have to guess?
